introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. English Language 2 (0730), June 2019, ADVANCED LEVEL. Paper 2: Section A - Summary and Text Reconstruction; Section B - Composition; Section C - Prescribed Texts. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Answer BOTH questions in SECTION A and ONE EACH from SECTIONS B and C in the SAME Answer Booklet, beginning each section on a new page. Begin with SECTION A.

Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks.

Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure considered as an attempt to cheat will earn you a penalty.

In the SUMMARY question, use mainly your own words. Indiscriminate copying of portions of the passage as your answer will earn you no marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

A pre-prepared or memorized composition will earn you no marks.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION B - COMPOSITION (20 marks)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (06 marks); Expression (08 marks); Accuracy (06 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write about from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly, and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity. You should write between 500 and 550 words.

figures.legende: Picture A: a street market scene (photograph) with an overflowing metal waste container and heaps of rubbish and vegetable waste around it, baskets of fruit and a black bucket on muddy ground, a woman in a white skirt on the left, and a motorcycle and shops on the right.
Picture B: a photograph, faint and misty, of four people seen from behind among tall maize plants in a field, with tall trees in the haze in the background.

questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Choose Picture A and describe what the eye sees (the overflowing skip, the baskets, the mud).
2. Introduce a character who knows this market (the aunt).
3. The consequences of the rubbish (flooding, flies, cholera).
4. The traders' action and the result.
5. Conclusion: the message of the picture.

**Model composition (534 words)**

Picture A shows a busy street market in the middle of a working day, but the first thing that strikes the eye is not the produce. It is the rubbish. A large metal skip stands against the stalls on the left, overflowing, and around it lie heaps of peelings, plastic bags, rotten vegetables and cartons that spill into the passage where shoppers must walk. In the foreground, baskets of fruit and a wide black bucket sit on bare, muddy ground, and in the distance a woman in a white skirt picks her way between the stalls. A motorcycle and a row of shops can be glimpsed on the right. I decided to write about what such a scene means for the people who live and trade there.

I know this scene well, for my aunt, Mami Ngwa, has sold tomatoes and vegetables in a market like this one for over twenty years. Every morning she arrives before six o'clock, arranges her baskets and greets her neighbours. For years she accepted the mess as a part of life. "The council collectors never come," she used to say, "and where else can we throw it?" Each evening the traders pushed their waste toward the skip, and each morning it was fuller.

The consequences were serious. In the rainy season, the rubbish blocked the gutters, and the water spread across the path, mixing with filth. Flies swarmed over the food, and a sour smell clung to clothes. Customers hesitated, and many went elsewhere. Then, one August, an outbreak of cholera struck the neighbourhood. Several traders, including Mami Ngwa's friend, fell ill, and two children were taken to hospital. The danger that had seemed only an inconvenience suddenly became a matter of life and death.

That crisis finally woke the market to action. A group of women, led by my aunt, called a meeting under the big tree. They agreed that complaining about the council would solve nothing unless the traders also changed their habits. They raised a small daily contribution, hired two young men to carry the waste to the collection point, set aside rotten produce for compost, and wrote to the mayor, demanding that the skip be emptied twice a week. Pupils of the nearby school painted signs reading "Keep our market clean" and joined the Saturday clean-up.

Within a month the transformation was clear. The skip no longer overflowed, the gutters flowed freely, and the smell vanished. Customers returned, and sales rose. The council, shamed by the women's letter, also began to collect the waste regularly. Mami Ngwa told me, laughing, that the market had once more become a place where people wanted to buy food, not a place where they feared to touch it.

The picture of piled rubbish, therefore, is not merely a scene of disorder; it is a warning and an invitation. It reminds us that a clean environment is not a luxury but the foundation of health and of decent trade, and that it begins with the determination of ordinary people to take responsibility for the place where they work. It is also a reminder to those who govern that public services cannot be left to the goodwill of traders alone.

**Marking grid**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 6 | Relevant ideas that answer the topic, developed with examples, in clear paragraphs with an introduction and a conclusion |
| Expression | 8 | Varied vocabulary and sentence structures, appropriate style and tone, fluent links between ideas |
| Accuracy | 6 | Correct grammar, tenses, spelling and punctuation |

**Common mistakes**

1. No clear link with the picture chosen, or not saying which picture is used.
2. Describing the picture line by line instead of building a composition from it.

incertitudes: Consigne de la page de garde (règle de choix) : « Answer BOTH questions in SECTION A and ONE EACH from SECTIONS B and C in the SAME Answer Booklet ». Section A obligatoire (aucune règle), Section B : 1 sujet sur 6 (a à f), Section C : 1 question sur 4. Les regles_choix sont identiques dans les 12 fichiers.

Fautes imprimées dans le sujet, laissées telles quelles : titre « SECTION A SUMMERY AND TEXT RECONSTRUCTION » (summary), « for few hours » (Q1), « A this stage », « into the will » (mill), « The stripped cane are then », « out of them » (Q2, forme reconstruite) ; Section C question 2 : « Use any Three prescribed text ».
Le tiret cadratin du passage de résumé (« choice of home - among the stinging tentacles ») est écrit « - » conformément à la règle du projet. Le passage ne porte pas de numéros de ligne imprimés.

Section A : le sujet imprime 30 marks pour la section (15 par question). La répartition des 15 points du résumé n'est pas imprimée : la grille du corrigé est indicative. La reconstruction est comptée à 1 point par blanc (15 blancs), ce qui est une hypothèse ; plusieurs réponses sont acceptables pour certains blancs (voir le corrigé).

Section B : 20 marks (Content and Organisation 6, Expression 8, Accuracy 6), 500 à 550 mots demandés. Points imprimés non corrigés. Compositions modèles : comptes de mots faits par script (de 517 à 534 mots).

Section B f) : les deux photographies (Picture A et Picture B) sont des demi-teintes photocopiées, voilées et peu contrastées ; elles sont reproduites par recadrage de la page sans filtre (aucun filigrane dans la zone de la photo). Picture A : scène de marché avec benne à ordures débordante, paniers de fruits, seau et passante (crédit imprimé « NDONGSON PHOTOS » et date 19/08/2018 en marge, partiellement conservés). Picture B : quatre personnes de dos dans un champ de maïs sous la brume, détails des visages et des vêtements illisibles. La composition modèle s'appuie sur Picture A.
